generatedProse.concept-context: Psychology gives the growth mindset a name and an evidence base, but the point is personal. When a statistics task or an essay feels beyond you, a fixed mindset reads it as a limit; a growth mindset reads it as something effort and better strategies can improve. Self-efficacy, your belief that you can succeed at a task, shapes whether you take a hard piece of work on or avoid it.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students each get a disappointing mark on their first essay.

Tom reads the grade and reaches the obvious conclusion: I am not cut out for psychology. The low mark feels like a verdict on fixed ability, so he quietly avoids the next challenging task and stops going to office hours, in case it confirms the worst. This is a fixed mindset, and the low self-efficacy that comes with it.

Amara is just as disappointed, but reads the mark differently: this attempt did not work, so what can I change? She studies the feedback, asks the tutor what a stronger essay would do, and treats the next task as a chance to improve. Her belief that effort will pay off, rather than being wasted, is self-efficacy at work. This is a growth mindset.

Both students met a setback. Only Amara read it as information to act on rather than a limit to accept.
generatedProse.summary: A growth mindset treats ability in psychology as something you can build with effort, strategies and feedback, where a fixed mindset treats it as set. Self-efficacy, the belief that you can succeed at a task, is its close partner and shapes whether you take a challenge on. You can now tell the two mindsets apart and identify a growth-mindset response to a setback. The next lesson turns to what drives your effort: your motivation.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara's reaction to the low mark show about self-efficacy?

items.text: She believed effort would pay off, so she acted on the feedback to improve.
She was sure psychology was simply too hard for her.
She decided the mark proved she lacked the ability.
She avoided the next task in case it went badly.

feedback.correct: That's right. Believing effort would pay off, and acting on it, is self-efficacy.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Self-efficacy is the belief that you can succeed with effort. Which option shows that?
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara showed self-efficacy by trusting that effort would pay off and acting on the feedback. The other options show low self-efficacy.
